cues.text: Let's build a feature in Korus.
I start a Mission and ask for cloud-based agents, alongside the local ones.
Before any code, I can review the requirements, clarify the scope, and approve the brief.
That becomes a set of tickets. I check the breakdown, then approve the work.
The agent works through each ticket in an isolated worktree. I can follow the progress and inspect the changes.
Next comes review. The findings get fixed one by one, then checked in another round.
I'm ready to hand this over. I'll create a pull request.
It's ready for my team to review.
From idea to delivery, in Korus.
I just finished working on a new feature. Let's review it.
I use the slash review command in my conversation.
I can keep the same model or choose another. Here, Claude reviews code written by Codex.
I enable automatic remediation for critical, high, and medium findings, and allow up to three review rounds.
Korus opens a new conversation with an independent reviewer. It checks the branch with fresh context.
These findings meet my priority threshold, so the fixes start automatically.
The agent fixes the issues one by one, and verifies each change.
A second review round starts automatically. This one comes back clear, so the loop stops.
The reviewer closes and returns its report to my original conversation. Changes stay uncommitted.
Review, fix, and verify automatically. From idea to delivery, in Korus.
Let's give this feature its own space.
I want a faster way to switch between agents. First, I talk it through.
A few iterations later, we've agreed on how it should work.
I can now use the slash delegate command to hand off the implementation.
Korus sets up the worktree, starts the agent, and hands over the instructions.
I keep working with the new agent. Here, I'm asking it to pin my recent sessions.
The changes are ready, so I select Merge. Korus brings them back and cleans up the worktree.
The agent closes. My first chat stays open.
I can keep discussing the feature, with my main branch clear.
I've got an idea for an app.
I start in Quick Chat, without a project folder.
I want to turn meeting notes into tasks. We discuss owners, due dates, and links back to the notes.
Once the idea is clear, I ask Korus to create the project.
It sets up the folder, creates a project agent, and hands over the plan we just worked out.
There's my new project. I can open its agent, and the original Quick Chat stays available.
The context is already here. I can start building.
From a conversation to a project, without starting over.
Let's see how this fits together.
I type slash visualize to get diagram suggestions on the right.
I'll open this release flow.
I select Annotate, then this box. I'd like to separate code review from human approval.
I send the annotation directly.
The agent uses my comment and the selected shape to update the diagram. Now review and approval are separate, and the rest stays in place.
I can show what I mean, right on the diagram.
Let's bring a teammate into the conversation.
I'm working on checkout retries. I share this conversation and send the invitation.
My teammate joins in Korus. The history is already here, and new updates arrive on both sides.
They suggest testing a payment that times out, then succeeds.
Their suggestion appears above my composer. I move it into my draft.
I add a regression test to the request, then send it to the agent.
We both see the fix and test results as the work progresses.
When we're done, I stop sharing. Their access ends.
Work together. Keep control. In Korus.
